content.title: About
content.content: Boston Cream Pie is a classic American dessert consisting of two soft sponge cake layers soaked with vanilla syrup, filled with a smooth custard cream, and topped with a chocolate glaze. Despite its name, it is a cake rather than a pie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dessert was created in the early 1900s and named after the city of Boston, where it first appeared in upscale restaurants.
In 1996, Boston Cream Pie was declared the official state dessert of Massachusetts.
The traditional recipe uses a custard made from eggs, sugar, milk, and vanilla, plus a dark chocolate glaze.
It is often served as bite‑size cupcakes known as Boston Cream Cupcakes.
Original sponge layers are lightly brushed with a simple syrup of water, sugar, and vanilla extract.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Milk and cream in the custard provide calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy contribute riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate glaze contains flavonoids that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cake contains milk and eggs, common allergens for some individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The dessert is rich in sugar, which can raise blood glucose levels and add extra calories.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some commercial chocolate glazes may contain partially hydrogenated oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boston Cream Pie is typically served in individual squares. It can be enjoyed chilled from the refrigerator or gently warmed to soften the chocolate glaze.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze it tightly wrapped for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before serving.

coffee-pre-sweetened-with-low-calorie-sw.title: Coffee, pre-sweetened with low calorie sweetener

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee is a beverage made from roasted and ground seeds of the coffee plant. This version is already pre‑sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener, allowing you to enjoy a sweet taste without extra calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee is the second most traded commodity in the world after oil.
There are over 100 coffee species, but commercially only Arabica and Robusta are widely cultivated.
Caffeine in coffee stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and mood.
Low‑calorie sweeteners such as stevia or erythritol are commonly used in diet products.
Coffee can be prepared in many ways: espresso, filter, French press, AeroPress, and more.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cognitive function
items.content: Caffeine improves attention, reaction time, and short‑term memory.

items.title: May reduce risk of certain diseases
items.content: Regular moderate coffee consumption is linked to lower risk of Parkinson’s disease and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Weight‑management aid
items.content: The low‑calorie sweetener provides sweetness without adding significant calories.

items.title: Boosts metabolism
items.content: Caffeine can increase metabolic rate, helping the body burn fat.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat with excessive coffee intake.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Coffee can irritate the gastric lining, especially on an empty stomach.

items.title: Allergy to sweetener
items.content: Rarely, people may have an intolerance or allergic reaction to the low‑calorie sweetener used.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain medications, such as stimulants or antidepressants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy coffee hot or cold, adding milk, cream, or aromatic spices to taste. The pre‑sweetened version is ready to drink without additional sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct light. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks to preserve aroma and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate chip cookie, reduced sugar is a soft, slightly crunchy cookie made with whole‑grain flour, a modest amount of natural sweeteners, and dark chocolate chips. It retains the classic chocolate chip flavor while containing about 30 % less sugar than traditional versions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cookie uses whole‑grain flour, increasing its dietary fiber content.
Sweetness comes from stevia and erythritol, which have minimal impact on blood glucose.
Chocolate chips are made from dark chocolate with at least 70 % cocoa solids.
The recipe was developed with nutritionists to lower the glycemic index.
No artificial colors or flavors are added.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Reduced sugar and natural sweeteners help maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidants from dark chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids, which may benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and iron
items.content: Whole‑grain ingredients supply minerals important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: Fats come mainly from chocolate and plant oils, making them healthier than in many conventional cookies.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie contains wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Chocolate allergy
items.content: Dark chocolate may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to cocoa.

items.title: Still contains sweeteners
items.content: Although sugar is reduced, the product still includes sweeteners, which may be undesirable on a strict sugar‑free diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a snack, crumble it over yogurt or ice cream, or incorporate it into dessert recipes such as layered cakes. Keep it in a dry place to preserve its crisp texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container at room temperature for 1‑2 weeks. For longer shelf life, refrigerate them, where they stay fresh for up to 1 month.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-made-with-bu.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg made with butter

content.title: About
content.content: An omelet or scrambled egg cooked in butter is a simple dish of beaten eggs gently fried in butter, which imparts a rich, creamy flavor. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, vitamin D, and essential minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Domesticated eggs have been used for over 7,000 years, originating in Southeast Asia.
Butter is about 80 % saturated fat but also supplies vitamins A, D, E, and K2.
The "scrambled" technique became popular in Europe in the 19th century as a quick way to cook eggs without a crust.
Slow cooking on low heat keeps the texture soft and preserves more nutrients.
In many cuisines the omelet is finished with herbs, cheese, or vegetables for added flavor.

items.title: Complete protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them an excellent source of high‑quality protein for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The yolk provides B12, riboflavin (B2) and pantothenic acid (B5), which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Eggs are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Choline in the yolk is essential for brain function and lipid metabolism.

items.title: Butter’s fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter supplies vitamins A, D, E and K2, which contribute to vision, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Butter is rich in saturated fats; excessive intake can raise LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with hyperlipidemia should monitor egg consumption.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; cook until the whites are fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet or scrambled eggs hot, garnished with fresh herbs, cheese, tomatoes or avocado. They work as a standalone breakfast, a sandwich filling, a wrap component, or a side to vegetable dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw eggs refrigerated at 1‑4 °C in their original carton. Cooked omelet should be eaten within 2‑3 hours at room temperature or stored in the fridge for up to 24 hours in an airtight container.
